statement: Debt valuation adjustment (DVA) reflects the firm's own default risk and can increase the value of a derivative to the firm when its own credit quality worsens.
explanation: DVA is the counterpart of CVA: it is the gain to a firm from its own possible default. When the firm's own credit worsens, DVA rises and increases the derivative's value to the firm.
originalText: PD = 15.35%; The CVA will increase, reflecting higher credit risk of the counterparty, reducing the derivative’s valuation, while DVA adjusts for the firm’s own risk, potentially increasing the value if its credit worsens.

statement: Debt valuation adjustment (DVA) is unaffected by the firm's own credit risk because it considers only market conditions.
explanation: DVA reflects the firm's own default risk, so it depends on the firm's own credit spread and not just on market conditions.
originalText: PD = 15.35%; The CVA will decrease as the counterparty’s credit risk is manageable, increasing the derivative’s valuation, while DVA remains unaffected as it only considers market conditions.

statement: Reduced-form models generate default correlation by assuming the hazard rates of firms follow stochastic processes correlated with macroeconomic variables, whereas structural models assume the firms' asset values follow correlated stochastic processes.
explanation: Each model class generates default correlation through a different channel: correlated hazard rates in reduced-form models and correlated asset-value processes in structural (Merton-type) models.
originalText: Reduced‑form models assume the hazard rates of the firms follow stochastic processes that are correlated with macroeconomic variables, whereas structural models, similar to Merton’s model, induce correlation by assuming the firms’ asset values follow correlated stochastic processes.

statement: Reduced-form models induce default correlation through correlated asset value processes, whereas structural models assume the firms' hazard rates are correlated with macroeconomic variables.
explanation: The mechanisms are the wrong way round: correlated asset-value processes belong to structural models, and hazard rates correlated with macroeconomic variables belong to reduced-form models.
originalText: Reduced‑form models induce default correlation through correlated asset value processes, whereas structural models assume the firms’ hazard rates are correlated with macroeconomic variables.
correction: Structural models induce default correlation through correlated asset value processes, whereas reduced-form models assume the firms' hazard rates are correlated with macroeconomic variables.

statement: Structural models ignore systematic factors, whereas reduced-form models capture common market and sector influences through correlated hazard rates.
explanation: Structural models do include systematic factors, because the firms' asset values follow correlated stochastic processes.
originalText: Structural models ignore systematic factors, whereas reduced‑form models capture common market and sector influences through correlated hazard rates.

statement: Reduced-form models can be calibrated to achieve any desired level of default correlation, whereas structural models can only produce low default correlations.
explanation: It is the other way round: structural models allow correlation to be set as high as needed, while reduced-form models achieve only a low range of default correlations.
originalText: Reduced‑form models can be calibrated to achieve any desired level of default correlation, whereas structural models can only produce low default correlations.
correction: Structural models can be calibrated to achieve any desired level of default correlation, whereas reduced-form models can only produce low default correlations.

statement: Structural models allow default correlation to be introduced through correlated stochastic processes for the firms' assets and to be set as high as needed, at the cost of longer computation time.
explanation: Because asset correlation can be set freely, structural models can represent a high probability of near-simultaneous default, for example of firms exposed to the same industry shock. The price is slow computation.
originalText: A structural model, because correlation can be introduced through correlated stochastic processes for the firms’ assets and can be set as high as needed, at the cost of longer computation time.

statement: Reduced-form models can produce a wide range of default correlations.
explanation: Reduced-form models achieve only a low range of default correlations, even though they are mathematically simple.
originalText: A reduced‑form model, because it is mathematically simple and the range of default correlations it can produce is wide.

statement: Structural models tend to take a long time to compute.
explanation: Structural models require modelling correlated asset processes, which is computationally heavy; this is their main drawback relative to reduced-form models.
originalText: Structural models tend to take a long time to process.

statement: Reduced-form models are more computationally intensive than structural models.
explanation: Reduced-form models are mathematically simpler and faster; structural models are the computationally heavy ones.
originalText: Reduced‑form models are more computationally intensive.
correction: Structural models are more computationally intensive than reduced-form models.

statement: Reduced-form models allow for very high default correlations.
explanation: Reduced-form models achieve only a low range of default correlations; structural models allow very high ones.
originalText: Reduced‑form models allow for very high default correlations.
correction: Structural models allow for very high default correlations.

statement: The effects of the economic cycle on default correlation trends are best reflected in structural models.
explanation: Economic-cycle effects are a strength of reduced-form models, whose hazard rates are correlated with macroeconomic variables.
originalText: Economic cycle impacts on default correlation trends are best reflected in structural models.
correction: The effects of the economic cycle on default correlation trends are best reflected in reduced-form models.

statement: Default correlation drives the shape of a credit portfolio's loss distribution: positive correlation makes defaults cluster, so credit risk cannot be fully diversified away and tail losses are larger than under independence.
explanation: Higher default correlation means defaults cluster, which fattens the tail of the loss distribution and limits the benefit of diversification.
originalText: Because default correlation drives the portfolio’s loss distribution: positive correlation makes defaults cluster, so credit risk cannot be fully diversified away and tail losses are larger than under independence.

statement: With positive default correlation, defaults of different obligors offset each other, so portfolio credit risk can be diversified away by adding more obligors.
explanation: Positive correlation means defaults tend to occur together rather than offset, so diversification is limited and credit risk cannot be fully diversified away.
originalText: Because with positive default correlation, defaults of different obligors offset each other, so portfolio credit risk can be diversified away by adding more obligors.

statement: Default correlation matters only for pricing single-name exposures and has no bearing on the loss distribution of a portfolio.
explanation: Correlation is irrelevant for a single name but is central to the loss distribution of a portfolio.
originalText: Because default correlation matters only for pricing single‑name exposures; it has no bearing on the loss distribution of a portfolio.

statement: Default correlation changes the expected loss of each obligor, while the variability of portfolio losses is unaffected.
explanation: Portfolio expected loss is the sum of the individual expected losses and does not depend on correlation; it is the spread and tail of portfolio losses that correlation changes.
originalText: Because default correlation changes the expected loss of each obligor, while the variability of portfolio losses is unaffected.

statement: The one-factor Gaussian copula approach converts the probability of default and the copula correlation into a 99.9% worst-case default rate, which is then multiplied by $L(1 - RR)$ to give the credit VaR.
explanation: The copula formula translates the unconditional PD and the correlation into a stressed default rate at the chosen confidence level; multiplying by exposure and loss given default gives the credit VaR.
originalText: Approach (i) converts the probability of default and the copula correlation into a 99.9% worst‑case default rate, which is multiplied by $L(1 - RR)$; approach (ii) simulates rating changes, so its losses include downgrades as well as defaults.

statement: CreditMetrics counts losses only from defaults, whereas the one-factor Gaussian copula approach also captures losses from rating downgrades.
explanation: The approaches are reversed: CreditMetrics captures downgrade losses, while the one-factor Gaussian copula formula captures defaults only.
originalText: Approach (ii) counts losses only from defaults, whereas approach (i) also captures losses from rating downgrades.
correction: The one-factor Gaussian copula approach counts losses only from defaults, whereas CreditMetrics also captures losses from rating downgrades.

changes.to: The one-factor Gaussian copula approach counts

changes.from: the one-factor Gaussian copula approach also

statement: In the one-factor Gaussian copula approach, the credit VaR is the unconditional default probability multiplied by $L(1 - RR)$, so the copula correlation does not affect it.
explanation: Correlation matters: the worst-case default rate rises with the copula correlation and exceeds the unconditional PD at high confidence levels, so ignoring it understates the credit VaR.
originalText: Approach (i) multiplies the unconditional default probability by $L(1 - RR)$, so the copula correlation does not affect the credit VaR.

statement: CreditMetrics samples the rating changes of different counterparties independently, which is why it is computationally quick.
explanation: CreditMetrics correlates rating changes through a Gaussian copula, with the correlation set equal to the equity return correlation, and it is computationally intensive.
originalText: Approach (ii) samples the rating changes of different counterparties independently, which is why it is computationally quick.

statement: A credit default swap is an insurance-type contract that protects the buyer against default of the underlying reference asset.
explanation: The CDS buyer pays a spread and the seller pays out on a credit event of the reference entity or asset.
originalText: To protect against the default of the underlying asset.

statement: An institution can reduce the credit risk of an asset by selling a large number of credit default swaps.
explanation: Selling CDS protection increases an institution's credit exposure; protection is obtained by buying CDS.
originalText: To reduce the individual risk of any asset by selling a large number of CDSs.
correction: An institution can reduce the credit risk of an asset by buying credit default swap protection.

changes.from: selling a large number of credit default swaps

statement: In a total return swap, one party pays the total return on a reference asset (coupons plus any gain or loss in value) and receives a floating rate plus a spread, so the other party gets the economic exposure of owning the asset without owning it.
explanation: The total return receiver obtains the asset's economic performance and pays a financing-type leg, giving synthetic, leveraged-like exposure to the asset.
originalText: Total return swap (TRS)

statement: A physically settled credit default swap exchanges the total return on a reference asset for a floating rate plus a spread.
explanation: Physical settlement is only a way of settling a CDS after default, by delivering the bond for par; it does not exchange total returns.
originalText: Physically settled CDS

statement: A collateralized debt obligation is a swap in which total return on an asset is exchanged for a floating rate plus a spread.
explanation: A CDO is a structure that tranches the credit losses of a portfolio of bonds or CDS; it is not a swap of total return for a floating rate.
originalText: Collateralized debt obligation (CDO)

statement: Selling protection through a single-name CDS is a long credit position that gains when the reference entity's credit quality improves and its CDS spread narrows.
explanation: The protection seller receives a spread that is now above the market spread and faces a lower chance of paying out, so the position gains like owning the bond.
originalText: Selling protection on the entity through a single‑name CDS

statement: A protection buyer in a single-name CDS gains when the reference entity's CDS spread narrows.
explanation: A protection buyer is short credit and gains when spreads widen, not narrow.
originalText: Buying protection on the entity through a single‑name CDS
correction: A protection buyer in a single-name CDS gains when the reference entity's CDS spread widens.

statement: A buyer of protection on a first-to-default basket CDS gains when the credit quality of the names in the basket improves.
explanation: A first-to-default protection buyer is short credit and benefits from deterioration in any name in the basket.
originalText: Buying protection on a first‑to‑default basket CDS that includes the entity
correction: A buyer of protection on a first-to-default basket CDS gains when the credit quality of a name in the basket deteriorates.

statement: A synthetic collateralized debt obligation arranges credit risk into tranches of different priority, each with its own risk-return profile.
explanation: A CDO structure allocates portfolio credit losses by seniority, so equity, mezzanine and senior tranches have different risk and return.
originalText: Synthetic Collateralized Debt Obligation (CDO).

statement: Under physical settlement of a credit default swap, the protection buyer delivers the defaulted bonds and receives their par value from the protection seller.
explanation: Physical settlement exchanges the defaulted bonds for par.
originalText: Under physical settlement the bank delivers the bonds and receives \$10 million.

statement: A bondholder who buys CDS protection on the full face value of the bonds is left with the face value after a default, whether the CDS is cash or physically settled (ignoring premiums).
explanation: With cash settlement the defaulted bonds are worth the recovery value and the CDS pays the loss, and together they equal par; with physical settlement the buyer receives par directly.
originalText: Whichever settlement is used, the bond‑plus‑CDS position leaves the bank with \$10 million of par value (ignoring premiums paid and accrued premium).

statement: The cash settlement payoff on a credit default swap equals the notional multiplied by the recovery rate.
explanation: A CDS pays the loss given default, notional multiplied by one minus the recovery rate, not the recovery value.
originalText: The CDS payoff to the bank is \$4.0 million, because the payoff equals the notional times the recovery rate.
correction: The cash settlement payoff on a credit default swap equals the notional multiplied by one minus the recovery rate.

changes.to: multiplied by one minus the recovery rate

statement: At the end of a total return swap, if the reference asset has fallen in value, the total return receiver pays the payer the amount of the decline.
explanation: The receiver bears the asset's price changes, so a fall in value is paid to the payer, in addition to the separate exchange of coupons and floating-rate payments.
originalText: The bank receives \$30 million from the hedge fund, since the receiver pays the decline in value.

statement: If the yield on a reference entity's bond rises because of a rating downgrade, the value of a long (protection buyer) CDS position increases.
explanation: A downgrade widens credit spreads, raising the market-implied default risk, so the protection becomes more valuable.
originalText: If the yield on Konkcore’s bond increases due to a rating downgrade, the value of the CDS will increase

statement: If the price of a bond falls because of a rise in interest rates, the value of CDS protection on that bond increases.
explanation: A rate-driven price decline is not a credit-spread move; a CDS hedges credit risk, not interest rate risk.
originalText: If the price of Konkcore’s bond decreases due to a rise in interest rates, the value of the CDS will increase

statement: If the default correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller increases, the value of the CDS to the protection buyer increases.
explanation: Higher correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller increases counterparty risk, which lowers the CDS value to the buyer.
originalText: If the default correlation between Konkcore and Counterparty increases, the value of the CDS will increase
correction: If the default correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller increases, the value of the CDS to the protection buyer decreases.

statement: When a credit default swap is cash settled after a default, the protection seller pays the buyer approximately the mid-market value of the defaulted bonds as determined by auction.
explanation: The payoff is the notional minus the auction-determined value of the defaulted bonds, that is, the loss, not the value of the defaulted bonds.
originalText: If Konkcore defaults on the bonds and settlement occurs in cash, the payoff on the CDS from Counterparty to Financial Bank is approximately the mid‑market value of defaulted bonds as determined by auction process several days after the credit event

statement: Buying CDS protection on a portfolio's constituents reduces credit risk by transferring the default loss on the reference entities to the protection seller without selling the underlying assets.
explanation: The protection buyer is compensated for default losses on the reference entities while keeping the assets.
originalText: buy protection in a credit default swap (CDS) on the portfolio constituents.

statement: An investor can reduce the credit risk of a portfolio by buying a CDO tranche.
explanation: Buying a CDO tranche makes the investor a taker of credit risk, so it increases exposure.
originalText: buy a collateralized debt obligation (CDO) tranche.

statement: An investor can reduce the credit risk of a portfolio by selling protection in an index CDS.
explanation: Selling protection means paying out on defaults of the index names, which adds credit risk rather than hedging it.
originalText: sell protection in an index credit default swap (CDS).

statement: An investor can reduce the credit risk of a portfolio by entering a total return swap as the total return receiver.
explanation: The total return receiver bears the asset's credit and market losses, replicating a leveraged long position in the asset.
originalText: enter into a total return swap (TRS) as the total return receiver.

statement: CDS spreads are calculated such that the present value of the expected payoff equals the present value of the expected payments over the life of the CDS.
explanation: A new CDS has zero initial value, so the spread is solved so that the PV of expected payoff equals the PV of expected regular and accrual payments.
originalText: expected payoff is equal to the PV of expected payments during the life of the CDS.

statement: CDS spreads are calculated such that the present value of accrual payments is zero.
explanation: The accrual payment is the pro rata premium owed on default between payment dates and is generally positive; it is part of the payments leg.
originalText: accrual payments is zero.

statement: CDS spreads are calculated such that the present value of the expected payoff is less than the present value of the expected payments over the life of the CDS.
explanation: A new CDS has zero initial value, so the PV of the expected payoff equals the PV of expected payments; a lower payoff PV would mean the buyer overpays.
originalText: expected payoff is less than the PV of expected payments during the life of the CDS.
correction: CDS spreads are calculated such that the present value of the expected payoff equals the present value of the expected payments over the life of the CDS.

statement: CDS spreads are calculated such that the present value of the expected payoff is greater than the present value of the expected payments over the life of the CDS.
explanation: A new CDS has zero initial value, so the PV of the expected payoff equals the PV of expected payments; a higher payoff PV would mean the buyer underpays.
originalText: expected payoff is greater than the PV of expected payments during the life of the CDS.
correction: CDS spreads are calculated such that the present value of the expected payoff equals the present value of the expected payments over the life of the CDS.

statement: If a CDS default is assumed to occur at mid-year rather than at year-end, the present value of the expected payoff is higher, because the payoff is discounted over a shorter period.
explanation: An earlier default time means a larger discount factor, so the PV of the expected payoff is higher for the same default probability and payoff.
originalText: It is higher, because the payoff is discounted over a shorter period.

statement: If a CDS default is assumed to occur at mid-year rather than at year-end, the present value of the expected payoff is lower, because the payoff is discounted over a longer period.
explanation: Mid-year is earlier than year-end, so the discounting period is shorter and the PV is higher.
originalText: It is lower, because the payoff is discounted over a longer period.
correction: If a CDS default is assumed to occur at mid-year rather than at year-end, the present value of the expected payoff is higher, because the payoff is discounted over a shorter period.

statement: In CDS valuation, the expected payoff in a period is the probability of default in that period multiplied by (1 - recovery rate) and by the notional.
explanation: The payoff on default is the loss given default, notional times (1 - R), weighted by the probability of default in that period and then discounted.
originalText: The probability of default in the period is multiplied by (1 ‑ recovery rate) and by the notional.

statement: In CDS valuation, the expected payoff in a period is the probability of default in that period multiplied by the recovery rate and by the notional.
explanation: That multiplies by R rather than (1 - R), so it measures the amount recovered instead of the amount the seller pays out.
originalText: The recovery rate is used as a direct multiplier of the probability of default and the notional.
correction: In CDS valuation, the expected payoff in a period is the probability of default in that period multiplied by (1 - recovery rate) and by the notional.

statement: In CDS valuation, the recovery rate is applied to the expected spread payments to estimate the actual cash flows.
explanation: Recovery affects the payoff leg, not the buyer's spread payments, which depend on survival.
originalText: The recovery rate is applied to the expected spread payments to estimate the actual cash flows.

statement: In the standard CDS valuation convention, defaults are assumed to occur at the midpoint of each payment period.
explanation: Defaults are assumed to occur midway between payment dates; this is simple and usually gives good results, and an accrual payment is due on default.
originalText: Defaults occur at the midpoint of each period.

statement: In the standard CDS valuation convention, defaults are assumed to occur at the start of each period.
explanation: The convention is that defaults occur midway between payment dates, not at the start of the period.
originalText: Defaults occur at the start of each period.
correction: In the standard CDS valuation convention, defaults are assumed to occur at the midpoint of each period.

changes.from: at the start of each period
changes.to: at the midpoint of each period

statement: In the standard CDS valuation convention, defaults are assumed to occur at the end of each period.
explanation: The convention is that defaults occur midway between payment dates, not at the end of the period.
originalText: Defaults occur at the end of each period.
correction: In the standard CDS valuation convention, defaults are assumed to occur at the midpoint of each period.

changes.from: at the end of each period
changes.to: at the midpoint of each period

statement: In the spread payments approach to valuing a synthetic CDO tranche, the tranche spread is the one that sets the present value of expected spread payments (on the declining tranche principal) equal to the present value of expected default-related payoffs.
explanation: The tranche spread is the breakeven that equates the PV of expected premium inflows with the PV of expected credit-loss payoffs, as for a single-name CDS.
originalText: Find the tranche spread that sets the PV of expected spread payments (on the declining tranche principal) equal to the PV of expected default‑related payoffs.

statement: The spread of every tranche of a synthetic CDO can be set equal to the average CDS spread of the reference entities.
explanation: The average pool spread is the aggregate across tranches; each tranche earns a spread that reflects its own seniority and risk.
originalText: Take the average CDS spread of the reference entities and apply it unchanged to every tranche.

statement: In the one-factor Gaussian copula model, a correlation parameter links the marginal default-time distributions of the reference entities, so that the distribution of the number of defaults, and hence tranche losses, can be derived.
explanation: The copula turns identical marginal default probabilities into a joint loss distribution, which is what differentiates equity, mezzanine and senior tranche values.
originalText: Link the marginal default‑time distributions of reference entities through a correlation parameter, so the distribution of the number of defaults, and hence tranche losses, can be derived.

statement: In the one-factor Gaussian copula model, defaults are independent unconditionally, so tranche losses follow a simple binomial distribution.
explanation: Independence holds only conditional on the common factor; unconditionally, defaults are correlated through that factor.
originalText: Assume defaults are independent so that tranche losses follow a simple binomial distribution unconditionally.

statement: The one-factor Gaussian copula model predicts which reference entity will default first and when.
explanation: The model gives probabilities of the number of defaults, not the identity or order of defaults.
originalText: Predict which reference entity will default first and when.

statement: In the one-factor Gaussian copula model, defaults of different entities are independent conditional on the common factor, so the number of defaults is binomial and the results are then integrated over the factor.
explanation: Conditioning on the common factor makes defaults independent, allowing a binomial calculation; correlation still enters through the conditional default probability and the integration over the factor.
originalText: Defaults of different entities become independent, so the probability of exactly $k$ defaults follows a binomial distribution; results are then integrated over $F$.

statement: In the one-factor Gaussian copula model, conditioning on the common factor eliminates correlation from the valuation, so the tranche price no longer depends on the correlation.
explanation: Correlation is embedded in the conditional default probability, so the tranche price still depends on it.
originalText: Correlation is eliminated from the valuation, so the tranche price no longer depends on $\rho$.

statement: To compute the expected loss and breakeven spread of a synthetic CDO tranche under the one-factor Gaussian copula model, conditional default probabilities and expected tranche principals are computed given the common factor and then integrated over the standard normal distribution of the factor.
explanation: Tranche values depend on the whole loss distribution, which is obtained by integrating the conditional (binomial) results over the common factor.
originalText: Compute conditional default probabilities and expected tranche principals given the common factor, then integrate these over the standard normal distribution of the factor.

statement: The unconditional default probability alone is enough to compute the expected loss of a synthetic CDO tranche.
explanation: The unconditional probability gives only the marginal default probability, not the distribution of the number of defaults, which depends on correlation.
originalText: Compute the unconditional default probability $Q(t)$ only and apply it directly to the tranche attachment points.

statement: At inception, the spread rate of each tranche of a synthetic CDO reflects its seniority, and the total spread payments across tranches equal the CDS premiums received on the reference pool.
explanation: Spread rates are priced to risk and decline with seniority, while the total dollar spread equals the pool's CDS premium.
originalText: each tranche’s spread rate reflects its seniority (risk), and the total spread payments across tranches equal the CDS premiums received on the reference pool.

statement: At inception, each tranche of a synthetic CDO earns the same spread rate.
explanation: Equal rates would ignore the different loss exposure: the equity tranche bears first losses and earns the highest rate, the senior tranche the lowest.
originalText: each tranche earns the same spread rate.

statement: Senior tranches of a synthetic CDO earn the highest spread rate because they have the largest notional.
explanation: The senior tranche has the largest notional but the lowest spread rate, because it is last to absorb losses.
originalText: senior tranches earn the highest spread rate because they have the largest notional.
correction: Senior tranches of a synthetic CDO earn the lowest spread rate because they are last to absorb losses.

changes.from: highest spread rate because they have the largest notional
changes.to: lowest spread rate because they are last to absorb losses

statement: The equity tranche of a synthetic CDO earns the lowest spread rate because it is the smallest tranche.
explanation: The equity tranche bears first losses and therefore earns the highest spread rate, regardless of its size.
originalText: the equity tranche earns the lowest spread rate because it is the smallest.
correction: The equity tranche of a synthetic CDO earns the highest spread rate because it bears first losses.

changes.from: lowest spread rate because it is the smallest tranche
changes.to: highest spread rate because it bears first losses

statement: The compound (tranche) correlation of a tranche is the correlation that makes the model-calculated spread for that tranche equal the spread quoted in the market, found by an iterative search.
explanation: Compound correlation is an implied correlation, analogous to implied volatility: it is backed out so that each tranche's model spread equals its market spread.
originalText: makes the model‑calculated spread for that tranche equal to the spread quoted in the market, found by an iterative search.

statement: Compound correlation is the correlation that prices the tranche running from zero up to the detachment point consistently with the market.
explanation: That describes base correlation; compound correlation targets a single tranche's spread.
originalText: makes the model price of the equity tranche $[0, a]$ consistent with the market, using the cumulative expected loss up to the tranche’s detachment point.
correction: Base correlation is the correlation that prices the tranche running from zero up to the detachment point consistently with the market.

statement: The compound correlation of a tranche is estimated directly from historical co-movements in the credit spreads of the reference entities.
explanation: Compound correlation is an implied correlation backed out of market quotes, not a historical estimate.
originalText: is estimated directly from historical co‑movements in the credit spreads of the reference entities.

statement: Base correlation is the correlation that makes the $\{0, a_{q}\}$ tranche price consistently with the market, with the tranche's expected loss built from the compound correlations of the tranches up to $a_{q}$.
explanation: Base correlation is defined for the tranche from zero to the detachment point and is built up from the expected losses implied by the compound correlations.
originalText: It is the correlation that makes the $\{0, a_{q}\}$ tranche price consistently with the market, with the tranche’s expected loss built from the compound correlations of the tranches up to $a_{q}$.

statement: Base correlation is the correlation that makes the model spread of the $\{a_{q-1}, a_{q}\}$ tranche equal its quoted spread.
explanation: That is the compound (tranche) correlation, which targets a single tranche between two attachment points.
originalText: It is the correlation that makes the model spread of the $\{a_{q-1}, a_{q}\}$ tranche equal its quoted spread.
correction: Compound correlation is the correlation that makes the model spread of the $\{a_{q-1}, a_{q}\}$ tranche equal its quoted spread.

statement: Base correlation is the average of the compound correlations of all tranches in the capital structure.
explanation: Base correlation is solved from the expected loss of the $\{0, a_{q}\}$ tranche; it is not an average of compound correlations.
originalText: It is the average of the compound correlations of all tranches in the capital structure.

statement: If market prices were consistent with the one-factor Gaussian copula model, the implied correlations would be the same for all tranches.
explanation: A pronounced smile or skew in implied correlations is inconsistent with a single-correlation Gaussian copula, which is a limitation of the model.
originalText: i, ii and iii only

statement: Base correlation and compound correlation are both implied correlations.
explanation: Both are backed out of market quotes for CDO tranches by an iterative search, like implied volatility.
originalText: implied correlations.

statement: Base correlation and compound correlation both exhibit a skew with correlations rising with tranche seniority.
explanation: Only base correlations show a skew rising with seniority; compound correlations show a smile.
originalText: exhibiting a skew with correlations rising with tranche seniority.

statement: Special purpose vehicles are designed to isolate a firm from financial risk, typically by transferring assets to the vehicle for management or by using it to finance a large project without risking the entire firm.
explanation: Asset transfer, project financing and risk isolation are the defining features of an SPV.
originalText: SPVs are designed to isolate a firm from financial risk, typically by transferring assets to the SPV for management or by using it to finance a large project without risking the entire firm.

statement: Derivatives product companies are legal entities created primarily for asset management and to finance large projects without exposing the entire firm to financial risk.
explanation: That describes an SPV. A DPC is a separately capitalised, bankruptcy-remote, typically triple-A dealer subsidiary used as a high-quality derivatives counterparty.
originalText: DPCs are legal entities created primarily for asset management and to finance large projects without exposing the entire firm to financial risk.

statement: Monolines and credit derivatives product companies are primarily used to change bankruptcy rules so that clients receive their full investment if a counterparty becomes insolvent.
explanation: Changing bankruptcy priorities (flip provisions) is an SPV feature. Monolines and CDPCs are leveraged guarantors and protection sellers that did not post collateral in normal times.
originalText: Monolines and CDPCs are primarily used to change bankruptcy rules so that clients receive their full investment if a counterparty becomes insolvent.

statement: Derivatives product companies are typically triple-A-rated, separately capitalised, bankruptcy-remote subsidiaries of a major dealer, giving counterparties a degree of protection against failure of the DPC's parent.
explanation: Separate capitalisation and bankruptcy remoteness from the parent allow a DPC to obtain a triple-A rating and shield counterparties from failure of the parent.
originalText: DPCs are typically triple‑A‑rated, separately capitalised, bankruptcy‑remote subsidiaries of a major dealer, which give counterparties a degree of protection against failure of the DPC parent.

statement: Derivatives product companies primarily change bankruptcy rules so that clients receive their full investment ahead of other claims if a counterparty becomes insolvent.
explanation: Altering bankruptcy priorities for investors (flip provisions) is an SPV mechanism, not the purpose of a DPC.
originalText: DPCs primarily change bankruptcy rules so that clients receive their full investment ahead of other claims if a counterparty becomes insolvent.

statement: Derivatives product companies hold no capital of their own, and their triple-A rating is always taken directly from the rating of the sponsoring parent.
explanation: DPCs are separately capitalised and maintain their rating through capital, margining and activity restrictions.
originalText: DPCs hold no capital of their own; their triple‑A rating is always taken directly from the rating of the sponsoring parent.

statement: Monolines were financial guarantee companies that provided 'credit wraps' and later also sold protection in the CDS and structured finance markets.
explanation: Providing credit wraps (financial guarantees) and then CDS and structured-finance protection is the defining business of monolines.
originalText: Monolines were financial guarantee companies that provided ’credit wraps’, and later also sold protection in the CDS and structured finance markets.

statement: Monolines were legal entities created to manage assets and finance large projects, isolating the entire firm from financial risk.
explanation: That describes a special purpose vehicle; monolines were guarantors that assumed credit risk for a premium.
originalText: Monolines were legal entities created to manage assets and finance large projects, isolating the entire firm from financial risk.

statement: The primary function of monolines was to act as structured entities designed to mitigate counterparty risk in OTC derivatives markets.
explanation: Monolines were guarantors who assumed credit risk for a premium, not bankruptcy-remote structures built to reduce counterparty risk like SPVs and DPCs.
originalText: The primary function of monolines was to act as structured entities designed to mitigate counterparty risk in OTC derivatives markets.

statement: Monolines evolved to allow counterparties with less than triple-A credit quality to trade long-dated derivatives.
explanation: Allowing sub-triple-A counterparties to trade long-dated derivatives was the original motivation for derivatives product companies, not monolines.
originalText: Monolines evolved to allow counterparties with less than triple‑A credit quality to trade long‑dated derivatives.

statement: Special purpose vehicles are commonly used in structured notes to guarantee counterparty risk on the note's principal to a very high (typically triple-A) level, and rating agencies examine their mechanics and legal specifics before granting a rating.
explanation: An SPV's rating depends on its legal mechanics, which is also why SPVs carry legal (consolidation) risk.
originalText: Special purpose vehicle (SPV)

statement: A special purpose vehicle can be designed to change bankruptcy priorities so that, if a counterparty is insolvent, a client can retrieve its full investment before other claims are paid.
explanation: Bankruptcy-priority engineering (flip provisions) and asset isolation are defining features of an SPV; DPCs, monolines and CDPCs do not rearrange bankruptcy priorities.
originalText: Special purpose vehicle (SPV)

statement: Monolines provide financial guarantees and were heavily involved in single-name CDS and structured finance, whereas SPVs typically manage assets or finance large projects to isolate firms from financial risk.
explanation: Monolines are guarantee and protection sellers, while SPVs are risk-isolating legal structures.
originalText: Monolines provide financial guarantees and were heavily involved in single‑name CDS and structured finance, whereas SPVs typically manage assets or finance large projects to isolate firms from financial risk.

statement: Special purpose vehicles are primarily used to provide 'credit wraps' in the credit derivatives market.
explanation: Credit wraps are the business of monolines, not SPVs.
originalText: SPVs are primarily used to provide ’credit wraps’ in the credit derivatives market, as monolines do.

statement: Both monolines and SPVs are legally obliged to post collateral against declines in the market value of their contracts because of their credit ratings.
explanation: Monolines and CDPCs typically did not have to post collateral in normal times because of their ratings, and nothing obliges SPVs to post collateral on this basis.
originalText: Both monolines and SPVs are legally obliged to post collateral against declines in the market value of their contracts because of their credit ratings.

statement: Both monolines and SPVs are designed to change bankruptcy rules so that clients can recover their full investment if a counterparty becomes insolvent.
explanation: Bankruptcy-priority changes are an SPV feature; monolines are insurers and do not alter bankruptcy rules.
originalText: Both monolines and SPVs are designed to change bankruptcy rules so that clients can recover their full investment if a counterparty becomes insolvent.

statement: In normal times monolines did not have to post collateral because of their triple-A ratings, but rating-downgrade clauses could force collateral posting just when their losses were rising.
explanation: Without collateral, protection relied entirely on the rating, and downgrade-triggered posting created a spiral in the financial crisis.
originalText: In normal times monolines did not have to post collateral because of their triple‑A ratings, but rating‑downgrade clauses could force collateral posting just when their losses were rising, so counterparties depended on the rating.

statement: The triple-A rating of a monoline effectively eliminates counterparty risk to it.
explanation: A triple-A rating lowers but does not eliminate counterparty risk; for monolines it collapsed in the global financial crisis.
originalText: The triple‑A rating effectively eliminates counterparty risk to a monoline.

statement: The triple-A rating of a monoline implies that it must post collateral against declines in the market value of its contracts.
explanation: Monolines typically did not post collateral in normal times; posting was triggered only by downgrades.
originalText: The triple‑A rating implies that the monoline must post collateral against declines in the market value of its contracts.

statement: Credit derivative product companies are safer than monolines because they exhibit right-way risk and do not create systemic risk.
explanation: CDPCs resemble monolines, are highly leveraged and were exposed to wrong-way risk rather than right-way risk; many failed.
originalText: CDPCs are safer than monolines because they exhibit right‑way risk and do not create systemic risk.

statement: Derivatives product companies reliably achieved an orderly, pre-packaged wind-down when their parents failed in the global financial crisis, removing counterparty risk for their clients.
explanation: DPC wind-downs in the crisis were not orderly: the Bear Stearns DPCs were wound down by JPMorgan after the parent's rescue and two Lehman DPCs filed for Chapter 11.
originalText: DPCs reliably achieved an orderly, pre‑packaged wind‑down when their parents failed in the global financial crisis, removing counterparty risk for their clients.

statement: A special purpose vehicle transforms counterparty risk into legal risk, since a bankruptcy court may consolidate the SPV's assets with those of the sponsor.
explanation: Substantive consolidation can defeat the isolation an SPV is meant to provide, leaving legal risk.
originalText: An SPV transforms counterparty risk into legal risk, since a bankruptcy court may consolidate the SPV’s assets with those of the sponsor.

statement: The protection offered by a derivatives product company proved weaker than expected because its fate was linked to its parent: the Bear Stearns DPCs were wound down by JPMorgan after the parent's rescue and two Lehman DPCs filed for Chapter 11.
explanation: The crisis experience showed that a DPC's high rating did not make it safe from the failure of its parent.
originalText: A DPC’s protection proved weaker than expected because its fate was linked to its parent: the Bear Stearns DPCs were wound down by JPMorgan after the parent’s rescue, two Lehman DPCs filed for Chapter 11, and DPCs also carry market and operational risk.

statement: A central counterparty structure spreads losses over a group of counterparties to minimize potential systemic risk.
explanation: A CCP uses collateralization and a default fund to mutualize losses across clearing members, whereas SPVs, DPCs and monolines concentrate risk in a single entity.
originalText: spreads losses over a group of counterparties to minimize potential systemic risk.

statement: A central counterparty structure enables a transaction originator to fail without affecting the other member firms.
explanation: In a CCP, a member's default does affect the other members through the default fund and loss mutualization; protection from a parent's failure is a feature of the DPC.
originalText: enables a counterparty transaction originator to fail and not affect the other member firms.

statement: Counterparty risk arises only when the contract has a positive net present value to the party facing the risk.
explanation: A loss on counterparty default occurs only where the surviving party has a gain on the contract, and that value is driven by market variables.
originalText: It arises only when the contract has a positive net present value (NPV) to the party facing the risk.

statement: Counterparty risk arises only when the contract has a negative net present value to the party facing the risk.
explanation: A negative-NPV contract is a liability to that party, so default by the counterparty does not create a loss for it.
originalText: It arises only when the contract has a negative net present value (NPV) to the party facing the risk.
correction: Counterparty risk arises only when the contract has a positive net present value to the party facing the risk.

statement: Because counterparty risk is a credit risk, it has no relationship to market risk.
explanation: Counterparty risk is a credit risk, but its size depends on market variables, so it is strongly linked to market risk.
originalText: Because it is a credit risk, it has no relationship to market risk.

statement: Counterparty risk is bilateral, because contract values can be positive or negative and so both counterparties face risk from the other.
explanation: Whichever party is 'winning' at the default date faces the risk that the 'losing' party defaults.
originalText: Counterparty risk is bilateral because cash flows can be negative or positive and both counterparties have a risk to the other counterparty.

statement: Counterparty risk is unilateral because only one counterparty bears a risk.
explanation: Unilateral risk describes lending, where only the lender is exposed; counterparty risk is bilateral.
originalText: Counterparty risk is unilateral because only one counterparty bears a risk.

statement: The future value of a derivative contract is certain.
explanation: The future value is typically highly uncertain because it depends on moving market variables; certainty would make the exposure resemble a loan.
originalText: The value of the contract in the future is certain.

statement: Unlike traditional lending risk, counterparty credit risk involves a future exposure that is highly uncertain and is often modelled using Monte Carlo simulation.
explanation: Highly uncertain, market-driven future exposure is the hallmark of counterparty risk, whereas lending risk involves a reasonably known amount.
originalText: She is employing Monte Carlo simulation because the future value of the contract is highly uncertain.

statement: Counterparty risk arises when a party stands to gain on a contract and another party must fulfil a contractual obligation.
explanation: A loss requires a gain (an asset) on the contract plus a counterparty that owes performance.
originalText: Counterparty risk arises when a party stands to gain on a contract and another party must fulfil a contractual obligation.

statement: Exchange-traded derivatives carry less counterparty risk than over-the-counter derivatives.
explanation: Exchange-traded contracts are centrally cleared and margined daily, which reduces counterparty risk.
originalText: Exchange‑traded derivatives carry less counterparty risk than over‑the‑counter (OTC) derivatives.

statement: Counterparty risk can be essentially eliminated if the trading partner is a prime broker.
explanation: Counterparty risk can be reduced by collateral, clearing and netting, but the identity of the counterparty does not remove it.
originalText: Counterparty risk can be essentially eliminated if the trading partner is a prime broker.

statement: Counterparty risk is typically associated with counterparty default prior to settlement rather than default during the settlement process.
explanation: By convention counterparty risk refers to default before final settlement (pre-settlement risk).
originalText: Counterparty risk is typically associated with counterparty default prior to the settlement rather than default during the settlement process.

statement: Over-the-counter derivatives contain less counterparty risk than exchange-traded derivatives because the counterparty is known.
explanation: Central clearing and daily margining make exchange-traded risk lower; knowing the counterparty does not reduce risk.
originalText: Over‑the‑counter (OTC) derivatives contain less counterparty risk than exchange‑traded derivatives because the counterparty is known.

statement: The precise future value of a derivative contract is uncertain, but the counterparties know whether the future value will be positive or negative.
explanation: Neither the amount nor the sign of the future value is known, which is why either party may end up exposed.
originalText: The precise future value of the contract is uncertain, but the counterparties are aware of whether the future value will be positive or negative.

statement: Credit exposure on a loan is approximately known and unilateral, while credit exposure on an interest rate swap is uncertain and bilateral, since either party may owe the other depending on rates.
explanation: Lending risk involves a known amount at risk and only the lender is exposed; derivative counterparty risk involves an uncertain amount and either party can be the creditor.
originalText: The loan exposure is approximately known and unilateral, while the swap exposure is uncertain and bilateral, since either party may owe the other depending on rates.

statement: At inception, the credit exposure on an interest rate swap equals its full notional amount.
explanation: A swap involves no exchange of principal, so its exposure is a variable fraction of notional, not the notional itself.
originalText: In the swap the exposure equals the full notional amount at inception, whereas in the loan the exposure is limited to the interest payments due.

statement: Settlement risk arises at final settlement because the two parties perform their obligations at different times, so one may pay while the other fails to deliver.
explanation: The timing difference creates a large but short-lived exposure.
originalText: The risk that arises at final settlement because the two parties perform their obligations at different times, so one may pay while the other fails to deliver.

statement: Settlement risk is the risk that a counterparty defaults at some point between trade inception and final settlement, causing loss of the remaining contractual payments.
explanation: That is presettlement risk, the usual meaning of counterparty risk.
originalText: The risk that a counterparty defaults at some point between trade inception and final settlement date, causing loss of the remaining contractual payments.
correction: Presettlement risk is the risk that a counterparty defaults at some point between trade inception and final settlement, causing loss of the remaining contractual payments.

statement: Settlement risk is the risk that a borrower fails to repay the principal amount of a loan.
explanation: That describes lending (credit) risk; settlement risk concerns the timing difference in performance at final settlement.
originalText: The risk that a borrower fails to repay the principal amount of a loan.

statement: Settlement risk generates potentially much larger exposures than presettlement risk, but default before the final settlement date is substantially more likely than default at settlement.
explanation: Settlement exposures are large but brief, while presettlement exposures are smaller but persist over the contract's life.
originalText: Settlement risk generates potentially much larger exposures, but default before the final settlement date is substantially more likely than default at settlement.

statement: Settlement risk generates much smaller exposures than presettlement risk, but default at settlement is much more likely.
explanation: The reverse holds: settlement exposures are potentially much larger but exist only briefly, so default at settlement is much less likely.
originalText: Settlement risk generates much smaller exposures than presettlement risk, but default at settlement is much more likely.

statement: In a repurchase agreement, a higher haircut (overcollateralization) reduces the counterparty risk faced by the lender.
explanation: A haircut gives the lender a cushion against borrower default and a fall in collateral value.
originalText: A higher haircut (overcollateralization) reduces the counterparty risk faced by the lender, Counterparty B.

statement: In a classic repo, the securities sold by the repo seller become collateral legally owned by the repo buyer, who can liquidate them to recover the cash lent if the seller defaults.
explanation: Title to the securities passes to the buyer.
originalText: The securities sold by Bank A become collateral legally owned by Counterparty B, who, if Bank A defaults, can liquidate them to recover the cash lent.

statement: In a repo, the repo seller bears no counterparty risk because it borrows cash; only the repo buyer is exposed.
explanation: Overcollateralization means the repo seller is itself exposed to the buyer failing to return the securities, so the risk is two-sided.
originalText: Because Bank A borrows cash, it bears no counterparty risk; only Counterparty B is exposed.

statement: In a repo, the lender is exposed to credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk, operational risk and legal risk.
explanation: The lender faces borrower default, collateral price volatility, illiquid collateral, operational failures and legal uncertainty.
originalText: Counterparty B is exposed to credit risk (default of Bank A), market risk (collateral price volatility), liquidity risk (illiquid collateral), operational risk and legal risk.

statement: On a CDS, the credit spread of the reference entity does not affect the protection buyer's exposure, whereas the credit spread of the protection seller does.
explanation: The CDS exposure is driven by the reference entity's spread. The protection seller's own spread reflects its default probability, which enters CVA rather than the exposure.
originalText: In regard to the exposure faced by Income Partners due to the CDS: the credit spread of Acme Corporation does NOT have an impact; however, the credit spread of Institutional Traders DOES impact this credit exposure

statement: In the bankruptcy of a derivatives counterparty, a derivative claimant will likely rank pari passu with the firm's senior unsecured bondholders.
explanation: Derivative claims normally rank with senior unsecured creditors.
originalText: In the event of a bankruptcy by Institutional Traders, Income Partners will likely be pari passu with the firm’s senior, unsecured bondholders

statement: Counterparty exposure on a derivative is measured gross of recovery, and the estimated recovery rate affects the quantification of counterparty risk through the credit value adjustment.
explanation: Recovery enters the loss through CVA, not the exposure itself.
originalText: Exposure faced by Income Partners, with respect to Institutional Traders, will be measured gross of recovery; but the estimated recovery rate will impact the quantification of counterparty risk via the credit value adjustment (CVA)

statement: Interest rate swaps account for the bulk of the notional amount outstanding in the OTC derivatives market.
explanation: They are far larger than credit default swaps, FX forwards and securities financing such as repos.
originalText: Interest rate swaps.

statement: Credit default swaps have a larger notional outstanding than interest rate swaps.
explanation: CDS notional is far smaller than interest rate swap notional.
originalText: Credit default swaps.

statement: A small derivatives player trades with few counterparties, specializes in one asset class, and posts collateral, if at all, that is often illiquid.
explanation: Sovereigns, large corporations and smaller financial institutions with specific hedging needs are typical small derivatives players.
originalText: A small derivatives player, because it trades with few counterparties, specializes in one asset class, and posts illiquid collateral if any.

statement: Small derivatives players are always required to post liquid collateral to dealers.
explanation: The collateral small players post, if any, is often illiquid.
originalText: A small derivatives player, because small players are always required to post liquid collateral to dealers to offset their lower trading volume.

statement: Large derivatives players trade with each other and with many clients, cover a very wide range of asset classes, and post collateral against their positions.
explanation: Large derivatives players are the large dealer banks.
originalText: Large players trade with each other and many clients, cover a very wide range of asset classes, and post collateral against their positions.

statement: Small derivatives players hold the largest number of OTC derivatives trades because they spread their activity across many asset classes.
explanation: Small players have few OTC trades and typically specialize in one asset class.
originalText: Small players hold the largest number of OTC derivatives trades because they spread their activity across many asset classes.

statement: Large derivatives players are typically sovereigns and corporations whose derivatives needs are specific and tied to a single asset class.
explanation: That describes small players; large players are the big dealer banks.
originalText: Large players are typically sovereigns and corporations whose derivatives needs are specific and tied to a single asset class.

statement: Firms that provide central clearing, trade compression and collateral management software are third-party providers of services that reduce counterparty risk and improve efficiency, rather than derivatives players that take on risk through trading.
explanation: Derivatives players take on counterparty risk through trading; clearing, compression and collateral services are offered by third parties.
originalText: The analyst is incorrect, because the firm is a third‑party provider of products and services that reduce counterparty risk and improve efficiency, not a derivatives player taking on risk through trading.

statement: Trade compression and collateral management services exist only inside large dealer banks.
explanation: These services are also provided by external third parties.
originalText: The analyst is correct, because trade compression and collateral management only exist inside large dealer banks.

statement: The higher the recovery rate from a counterparty, the lower the loss given default.
explanation: Loss given default is 1 minus the recovery rate, so the two move inversely, one for one.
originalText: The higher the recovery rate from the counterparty, the lower the loss given default amount.

statement: The higher the recovery rate from a counterparty, the higher the loss given default.
explanation: Loss given default equals 1 minus the recovery rate, so it falls as recovery rises.
originalText: The higher the recovery rate from the counterparty, the higher will be the loss given default amount.
correction: The higher the recovery rate from a counterparty, the lower the loss given default.

statement: The recovery rate from a counterparty always equals the loss given default.
explanation: They sum to 100%; they are equal only in the special case of a 50% recovery rate.
originalText: The recovery rate from the counterparty will always be equal to the loss given default amount.

statement: If a counterparty defaults while the contract's value to an institution is negative, the institution still owes the amount and is legally obliged to settle it.
explanation: Credit exposure is asymmetric: a positive value is a claim on the defaulted counterparty, while a negative value remains a liability the survivor must pay.
originalText: The institution owes the amount and is still legally obliged to settle it.

statement: If a counterparty defaults while the contract's value to an institution is negative, the institution is released from its obligation and does not need to settle the amount it owes.
explanation: The institution remains obliged to pay what it owes; it cannot gain from the counterparty's default except in special non-standard cases.
originalText: The institution is released from its obligation and does not need to settle the amount it owes.

statement: Loss given default represents the amount of exposure expected to be lost in the event of counterparty default.
explanation: LGD is 1 minus the recovery rate and multiplies exposure and default probability in the CVA calculation.
originalText: The amount of exposure expected to be lost in the event of counterparty default.

statement: Loss given default represents the amount of exposure expected to be recovered in the event of counterparty default.
explanation: That describes the recovery rate, the complement of LGD.
originalText: The amount of exposure expected to be recovered in the event of counterparty default.
correction: Loss given default represents the amount of exposure expected to be lost in the event of counterparty default.

statement: Loss given default is the probability of counterparty default given that it defaulted on a previous contract.
explanation: LGD is a loss severity, not a conditional default probability.
originalText: The probability of counterparty default given that it defaulted on a previous contract.

statement: Credit migration is crucial to measures of credit exposure because it affects the term structure of default probability.
explanation: Counterparty risk must be assessed over the whole life of the trades, and migration determines how default probability evolves over that horizon.
originalText: Because it impacts the term structure of probability

statement: Credit migration has no impact on credit exposure.
explanation: Migration changes the term structure of default probability and can cause problems even before a default.
originalText: None of the above: credit migration has no impact on credit exposure

statement: The replacement cost of a derivative contract is unlikely to equal its mark-to-market value exactly, but it is often approximated by the mark-to-market value.
explanation: Replacement cost differs from MtM because of costs such as bid-offer spreads, but MtM is the usual approximation.
originalText: Replacement cost is unlikely to equal exactly the MtM but is often approximated by the MtM
